stories.topic: Sara Rai: 'We Had Nothing Else to Do'
stories.summary: While recording with the writer Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand's granddaughter, Amit noticed that her childhood memories were so precise and evocative they sounded like crafted fiction. He asked how she remembered so much. She said they had nothing else to do, so they looked at things. Amit adds that when he asks guests his age about their childhood daydreams, some say they never daydreamed, which baffles him.
stories.insight: Attention is what memory is made of. In the 70s and 80s books, music and films were scarce but time was plentiful, so attention settled on the world. Today, with endless scrolling, deep observation and daydreaming take deliberate effort.
stories.quote: And I said, Sara how do you remember so much? And she was like, we had nothing else to do. So we looked at things.

stories.topic: Mixtapes for the Girl He Later Married
stories.summary: Amit brings out a TDK and a Sony cassette. They are mixtapes he made at nineteen for the seventeen-year-old he was wooing, whom he later married. Making one meant finding hard-to-get music from abroad, working a double-deck player, calculating how many minutes of songs fit on a side, and sitting through every track in real time.
stories.insight: The hours of effort were themselves the message: this is who I am, and I want you to like it. Choosing what to share also forced him to work out what he loved and why. A Spotify playlist made in a minute carries neither signal.
stories.quote: You are basically saying to them, at one hand, this is who I am, and at the other hand, that I want you to like this, right?

stories.topic: Meeting a Forgotten Younger Self in an Old Letter
stories.summary: Amit found a letter he had once written by hand, to someone he no longer remembers. It contained the plot of a story he was planning to write. He generally recalls his younger self as shallow and dislikes him, but the letter showed someone thoughtful he did not expect.
stories.insight: Written records can correct how we misremember ourselves. Memory may be choosing the wrong highlights, and old letters are evidence that can push back.
stories.quote: And it's fascinating to now look back at the younger me and think that that's another person entirely. Not in a bad way.

stories.topic: Letters to a Friend Two Buildings Away
stories.summary: In Class 8, Ajay and his friend Manisha Purohit sat a desk apart in school and lived two buildings apart in Bandra East. They still started writing each other letters and posting them.
stories.insight: Writing is a different register from talking. Even between people who see each other every day, a letter gets a level of care and attention that conversation does not.
stories.quote: Just you're living two buildings away. But it's a delight to write and get those physical pieces of paper

stories.topic: How CMIE Began with a Stack of Inland Letters
stories.summary: On 13 April 1976 Ajay's father was sacked. He came home, said so, and announced he would start a new organisation called CMIE. That same evening he wrote inland letters to friends all over India explaining what had happened and asking each of them for specific help.
stories.insight: An institution was started by handwritten requests to a network of friends. Each message was costly to send and so carried a full story and a clear ask. That is the opposite of today's cheap, shallow messages.
stories.quote: And that's how like CMIE got started with handwritten inland letters sent out to friends all over the country saying, Help me, I'm trying to do this.

stories.summary: Every steel almirah in Amit's childhood home was left unlocked except the one in his father's study. Amit found the hidden key and opened it. Among video cassettes and books were Playboy and Mayfair magazines. He brings two Playboys from 1967, when his father was about 26. Amit notes that Playboy published great short fiction. A treasured anthology of its stories is where he first read Murakami ('The Second Bakery Attack'), alongside Updike, Cheever and Nabokov. In the 1980s, he says, the two prestige outlets for a short story were The New Yorker and Playboy.
stories.insight: Before the internet, what people imagined about romance and sex came from Bollywood or a locked cupboard, so a single magazine carried huge weight. The magazine itself also shows that high literature and racy content often sat in the same pages.
stories.quote: there's this old saying where people will joke, I read Playboy for the stories. No, the thing is I actually did, because Playboy had a great tradition of publishing great short stories by the world's best writers.

stories.summary: Amit's father, a government servant, received free diaries every year. Knowing his son wanted to be a writer, he passed them on and told him to write his book. In the 1986 diary, twelve-year-old Amit began a novel called Tales of St. John's, wrote a couple of chapters, and stopped.
stories.insight: For Amit the diary stands for all the writing he never did. It also points to a privilege he never noticed: in many families paper itself was scarce, and without pages to fill and throw away you cannot write enough to get good.
stories.quote: I noticed that at that time at the age of twelve, I started writing this novel called Tales of Saint Johns and part one, chapter one is titled Tantalising Tantrums, which at least alliterates.

stories.topic: A Mother's Last Recipes and a Grandmother's Recipe Book
stories.summary: Amit's mother died of pancreatic cancer in 2008. Knowing she was dying, she wrote out by hand the recipes for everything he liked; a liver recipe is a particular favourite. When he cleared out his father's house, he also found his maternal grandmother's recipe book from around the 1960s. It is written in beautiful English and has both Western and Indian recipes.
stories.insight: Handwritten recipes show a person's inner life. For a woman whose world was constrained, collecting and recording recipes was creative work rather than drudgery. A handwritten recipe can also be an act of love. YouTube's endless free recipes cannot carry that.
stories.quote: She knew she was going to go. So before she went, she painstakingly wrote down recipes of all the stuff I liked and gave it to me.

stories.topic: Narendra Shenoy's Half-Hour on Michael Porter
stories.summary: Amit retells a story from his episode with Narendra Shenoy. In his arranged marriage to Sheila, Narendra felt pressure because Sheila's twin sister was paired with a great talker. Sheila even asked whether he had anything to talk about. So when Narendra, studying for an MBA in another city, called her long distance, he spent half an hour on the business philosophy of Michael Porter.
stories.insight: An expensive, scheduled long-distance call made you feel you had to say something meaningful. That pressure produced some very awkward results.
stories.quote: So our man calls Sheila, and he feels the unstated pressure to be interesting. So for half an hour he tells her about the business philosophy of Michael Porter.

stories.topic: The Badminton Girl Who Needed an 'Urgent' Call
stories.summary: Amit came to Fergusson College straight from a boys' school and could not read signals from girls. A girl he played badminton with turned up at his door with a friend and asked to use his phone for an urgent call. She made the call and left. Only years later did he realise it was probably an expression of interest.
stories.insight: The shared landline at a fixed address gave people ways to flirt that no longer exist. To read your own past correctly, you need to understand how things worked back then.
stories.quote: And it took me many years to kind of figure out that this was some kind of expression of interest in some way, because why the hell would you go into a random person house?

stories.topic: The Hostel Payphone and the Shouting Watchman
stories.summary: At Ajay's IIT Bombay hostel, everyone shared one coin payphone, and people queued to use it. For incoming calls, the watchman answered, heard 'I want to speak with Ajay Shah of 262', and went shouting '262' until Ajay ran down.
stories.insight: Payphones on street corners, and the shared routines that grew up around them, have disappeared completely. Being called was once a public event.
stories.quote: the watchman would come shouting two six two and then you would run down and pick up the phone.

stories.summary: Ajay's father bought the Survey of India map of India in four sheets, built a wooden board of the right size, and pasted them into a map about three metres by three metres on a wall at home. Whenever a place or river came up, the children climbed up to look. Ajay has tried for years to assemble a similar wall-sized map of the Himalayas without success, and asks listeners for leads.
stories.insight: A large map that is always on the wall makes geography part of daily family life. It gives an overall strategic sense of a place that phone maps lack.
stories.quote: And then it was just like standard operating procedure for us that any place names would appear, a river would appear, and like little kids would scamper up to the map and look at things and I miss that.

recommendations.item: Sara Rai Inhales Literature (Episode 255 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Brought up at the start, where Amit recalls how vividly Sara Rai remembered her childhood.
recommendations.reason: Her recollections are so precise they read like fiction. The conversation shows what attention was like before constant distraction.

recommendations.item: Chandrahas Choudhury's Country of Literature (Episode 288 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Mentioned while discussing letters; Amit says novelist Chandrahas Choudhury still sends him long, story-filled emails like the letters of old.
recommendations.reason: A conversation with a fine novelist who still writes emails the way people once wrote letters.

recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Ajay cites it as letters Nehru wrote to his daughter that together became a book.
recommendations.reason: Ajay ranks it among the world's great intellectual works and as proof that letters written with care can become a book.

recommendations.creator: J.R.R. Tolkien
recommendations.context: Mentioned alongside Nehru's book: Tolkien's letters to his children turned into The Hobbit.
recommendations.reason: Another case of writing for your family becoming something the world reads.

recommendations.item: Playboy Stories: The Best of Forty Years of Short Fiction
recommendations.creator: Alice K. Turner (editor)
recommendations.context: Amit calls it one of his treasured books, bought around 1998 or 1999. It is where he first read Murakami ('The Second Bakery Attack'), along with Updike, Cheever and Nabokov.
recommendations.reason: It shows why 'I read it for the stories' was literally true: Playboy published some of the best short fiction by top writers.

recommendations.creator: Larry Page and Sergey Brin (interviewed by Playboy)
recommendations.context: Ajay chips in during the Playboy discussion that the magazine ran an interview with Larry Page and Sergey Brin.
recommendations.reason: Evidence that Playboy carried serious long-form journalism alongside its fiction.

recommendations.item: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
recommendations.creator: Robin Dunbar
recommendations.context: Amit explains Dunbar's number (about 150 people, with about five close friends and a wider circle up to about twenty) while describing an old address book. He notes Dunbar has a book on it.
recommendations.reason: The source of the idea that an old address book was a physical record of everyone you knew.

recommendations.creator: Neil Young
recommendations.context: Ajay starts his 'one-way journeys' point with 'I was thinking about what a friend once said' and later finishes it with the Neil Young line 'I was hoping it was a lie.'
recommendations.reason: A lyrical touch Ajay uses during the conversation, and the song is linked in the show notes.

recommendations.creator: Wah Chef
recommendations.context: While contrasting handwritten family recipe books with today's endless cooking videos, Amit names Toddy Chicken as his favourite and promises a link.
recommendations.reason: His favourite cooking video, given as an example of how abundant recipes are now.

recommendations.item: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (Episode 250 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The episode where Narendra Shenoy told the story of spending a long-distance call to his future wife on Michael Porter.
recommendations.reason: Has the full version of that story and more from a funny, self-deprecating storyteller.

recommendations.item: Creative destruction (column on the demise of STD booths)
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik
recommendations.context: Ajay calls it a great newspaper column on how mobile roaming wiped out India's STD-booth industry.
recommendations.reason: A clear Indian example of creative destruction: an industry of over a million booths vanished, and people moved on to other jobs.

recommendations.item: Maps Are Magic (Episode 44 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit recalls it when Ajay talks about missing paper maps.
recommendations.reason: Their earlier full episode on maps, for anyone who wants more on the subject.

recommendations.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
recommendations.context: Amit invokes Borges after Ajay's search for a perfect wall map of the Himalayas.
recommendations.reason: Borges's fable of a map as big as the territory it shows, used as a joke about Ajay's search for a perfect map.

recommendations.creator: The Replacements
recommendations.context: Comes up through answering machines. Amit calls it the best album named Let It Be, with the Beatles in second place.
recommendations.reason: Amit rates this early-80s album above the Beatles' album of the same name.

recommendations.creator: The Replacements
recommendations.context: From Let It Be, with what Amit calls the immortal line 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?'
recommendations.reason: A sad, touching song that only makes full sense if you remember living with answering machines.

recommendations.item: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Ajay cites what Vitalik Buterin said to him and Amit in Madras when he argues for cash.
recommendations.reason: Background for the case that cash's anonymity and universal acceptance protect freedom.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit describes how the course has participants journal daily on a set subject, on condition that the journal stays completely private.
recommendations.reason: It builds the habit of private, unfiltered writing, which Amit says is how you discover what you think.

core_ideas.concept: We Shape Our Objects, Then Our Objects Shape Us
core_ideas.explanation: An object is more than its function. Whole patterns of behaviour and culture grow around it: making mixtapes, posting letters, queueing at STD booths. When the object disappears, that whole world goes with it, and that loss is more than nostalgia.
core_ideas.quote: We shape our objects and then our objects shape us in ways that go far beyond the simple functionality.

core_ideas.concept: The Last Time You Did X
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay suggests imagining that you could know, at the time, that this was the last day you would use a given object or do a given thing. These objects left our lives one by one without anyone noticing. Only in hindsight do we see that something big changed.
core_ideas.quote: One by one, as these objects have dropped out of our lives, in the moment we didn't even realize that this is gone.

core_ideas.explanation: In the 70s and 80s, books, music and films were scarce but time was plentiful, so people daydreamed and noticed things. Today everything is abundant except time, and we live in what Amit calls a shallow rhythm of scrolling and swiping. He presents this as a lament about himself, not a complaint about young people.
core_ideas.quote: Because the one scarcity that was not so acute as today was time. We had a lot of time.

core_ideas.explanation: Mixtapes, handwritten letters, and trips to the post office cost real time, and that cost showed the other person you cared. Ajay adds that this effort focused the mind and produced something beautiful, while easy access to everything makes focus harder. One modern fix he suggests: share songs in a careful email that tells the story around them.
core_ideas.quote: These are not trivial things, you're not hitting a button. It tells you that I care about you.

core_ideas.concept: Writing and Curating Shape the Self
core_ideas.explanation: Choosing songs for a mixtape, or writing a letter, makes you work out who you are. Writing does not just express thoughts you already have; it creates them, as Joan Didion said. So Amit urges people to journal daily and privately, so they can think without filtering. Letters also push you to turn your life into a story.
core_ideas.quote: when you write, you're not only expressing yourself, you are shaping yourself.

core_ideas.concept: Longhand Slows the Mind into Contemplation
core_ideas.explanation: Historians can read Nehru's and Patel's letters, but today's leaders mostly do not write letters at all. Writing by hand is slower, you feel the letters form, and it is hard to go back and edit. The hosts argue this puts you in a contemplative state and demands more brainpower than typing.
core_ideas.quote: And as he is writing, he is in that slow state of mind where he's contemplative, he's taking the time.

core_ideas.concept: An Email Can Still Be a Letter
core_ideas.explanation: The medium does not stop us from writing long letters; habit does. A Gmail draft can be edited for days before sending. Ajay and Lant Pritchett exchange 3,000-word emails, where a reply can take a month, as a conversation lasting years. A 'long form' subject line signals to the reader that this is not an everyday email.
core_ideas.quote: Gentle reader, you should know that when you write an email in Gmail, you're not obliged to punch send right there. It is stored in a folder that is called drafts.

core_ideas.concept: Paper as Privilege, Volume as Craft
core_ideas.explanation: Getting good at writing takes many attempts, and that requires having enough paper to write a lot and throw much of it away. For many families notebooks were scarce. Scarcity makes us value things more, but it can also freeze us, because when pages are precious, the urge to make every page perfect stops you writing at all.
core_ideas.quote: If you're not actually writing, writing, writing, writing a lot, writing so much that it can be thrown away. You know, you don't really have anything.

core_ideas.explanation: An old household address book held roughly a Dunbar's number of people (about 150) plus the grocer, electrician and plumber, all in one physical book kept in one place. Picking it up reminded you who was in your life. Without that reminder, people drift apart unless we keep up friendships on purpose.
core_ideas.quote: This is a physical manifestation of all the people you know in the world with their phone numbers.

core_ideas.explanation: For most of history, a person leaving might never be heard from or seen again: there were no phones, letters barely got through, and shipwrecks were a real risk. Constant contact and safe travel have ended that. Relationships are no longer suddenly cut off by a departure.
core_ideas.quote: In today's world, there are no one way journeys that a person never leaves because you're always in contact with them.

core_ideas.explanation: Religions reflect the customs of the societies they grew in. Amit reads the old Hindu ban on overseas travel as elders' fear that the young would leave and never return; even Bombay to Kanpur could take a month. He reads bans on pork as protection against disease from badly cleaned meat. Writing such rules into religion made them stick.
core_ideas.quote: And one way to read it is that the elders were terrified that somebody young would go overseas and they would never come back.

core_ideas.explanation: When calls meant a weekly trip to an STD booth, you felt you had to have a real conversation. Now you can reach anyone at any time, so there is no urgency and messages turn trivial. Ajay adds that asynchronous messaging, where the other person reads it later, is a new mode altogether, different from both no contact and live talk.
core_ideas.quote: Asynchronous messaging is a very different frame of mind compared to either nothing or synchronous.

core_ideas.concept: Creative Destruction: The STD Booth Wipeout
core_ideas.explanation: More than a million STD booths employing millions of people disappeared once mobile roaming arrived. Ajay argues that in a dynamic market economy like India's, job loss is usually not the disaster it sounds like, because people move on to other work.
core_ideas.quote: Most of the time in India, job loss is not a problem because there is a creative dynamic market economy and people move on, they get other jobs

core_ideas.concept: Paper Maps Show the Big Picture
core_ideas.explanation: Old Bartholomew or National Geographic maps were designed to hang on a wall, with labels and keys that show the world as a whole. Google Maps is designed for navigation, and even on a big screen its labelling does not give the same overview. Ajay notes that children today cannot read or fold a paper map.
core_ideas.quote: I think that there is a strategic sense that you see in a paper map that you don't see on Google Maps.

core_ideas.explanation: Cash is accepted almost everywhere and is anonymous. In a fully electronic system every transaction can be traced, and you live under constant watch. Ajay points to places like China where cash acceptance has broken down, and cites Vitalik Buterin. He argues that using cash is a civic duty.
core_ideas.quote: Gentle reader, use cash more. It's your social responsibility to use cash more.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's practical upgrade: share a QR code linking to a URL that hosts your contact file (VCF). Google Contacts checks that URL periodically, so other people's copy of your details updates automatically and never goes out of date.
core_ideas.quote: In the modern world, you're supposed to have a QR of the URL of your VCF file.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay shows up hoarse and Amit with a huge bag. Amit: 'I have a new voice for you in my bag, so in case your voice goes...' and then admits he's kidding.
Amit on his mixtape record: he made them for friends too, 'But as far as people you are wooing is concerned, hundred percent strike rate.'

Amit proposes on air an Everything is Everything newsletter where the two take turns writing long letters to each other. Ajay turns it down: 'But we talk too much. You also need a little starvation of connection.'
Working out that his father was turning 26 in November 1967, Amit suggests the Playboy issue 'might have been his twenty-sixth birthday gift for him, just imagine.'

Editor Nomsita leafs through a 1967 Playboy article on psychedelic drugs. Ajay: 'Is she underage for psychedelic drugs?' Amit: 'Nobody is underage for psychedelic drugs. So I've never had any. I'm just saying random things.'
Ajay admits he never read Biggles. Amit: 'Shocking. Your education is incomplete.'
Amit has a late-80s VHS of himself, very thin and shirtless, recorded on a camcorder, but no player. 'I'm not gonna trust any of you with that precious footage. So it will remain lost forever.'
Amit kept buying Filofaxes to organise his life and never using them. Ajay: 'Gentle reader, he was thinking about productivity all along.' Amit: 'I'm failing at productivity all along.'

Asked how he stores recipes, Ajay explains that as a PhD student he and Susan devised a text-file format for recipes and wrote an awk program to convert it into a LaTeX PDF recipe book. Amit can only respond: 'Sashtang pranam.'
At MTV Amit found 'writer' too boring as a job title, so his visiting card said 'Creative Animal.' When promoted, he asked what comes above Creative Animal and got 'Manic Beast.'
At a college STD booth, a new student from UP greets his mother with a formal 'Pranam, Mataji', and everyone at the booths turns to stare: 'What the fuck happened?'

Amit asks how push-button phones changed friendship. Ajay's answer is that you no longer memorised numbers. Amit: 'Good answer, but not the full answer.' His version: zero took the most effort to dial on a rotary phone, so friends with zeros in their numbers suffered.

Ajay twists the old saying 'What Bengal thinks today, India thinks tomorrow': 'What Bengal thinks today the rest of India hopes will never happen to them.' He then tells of a woman in Calcutta who picked up a crossed line and heard two strangers talking about her. Amit: 'Only in Calcutta.'
After Ajay's long search for a perfect Himalayan wall map, Amit invokes Borges: 'the only accurate map of the Himalayas would have to be as big as the Himalayas. So where are you gonna get that?'

Amit on The Replacements' Let It Be: 'the best album called Let It Be. The Beatles are in second place.' He adds that the line 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?' is lost on a generation asking 'What the fuck is an answering machine, dude?'
The episode was inspired by a tweet asking what has gradually disappeared over the last twenty years without anyone really noticing.
Joan Didion: 'I don't know what I think until I write it down.' Amit uses it to argue that writing is how you think, and to explain why the Life Lessons course requires private daily journaling.
When Amit wonders where earlier generations even got pens and ink, Ajay quips 'In what furnace was thy brain?', a line from William Blake's 'The Tyger.'
Ajay starts the 'one-way journeys' idea with 'I was thinking about what a friend once said' and later finishes it with 'I was hoping it was a lie', echoing Neil Young's 'After the Gold Rush.'

The shared reading list of a 70s/80s Indian childhood: Enid Blyton (The Mystery of Banshee Towers, the Five Find-Outers, the Secret Seven), the Hardy Boys by 'Franklin W. Dixon' (whom Amit recalls was a group of writers rather than one person), Biggles, and Alfred Hitchcock and the Three Investigators. Amit's point is that scarcity meant a whole generation read the same books.
TV of the early 80s: a Televista black-and-white set on four little legs, Doordarshan as the only channel, Chitrahaar once a week, and Alfred Hitchcock Presents, all watched at fixed times.
In 1967 India had no local men's magazines; Debonair came later. Amit also notes that in the 1980s the two prestige outlets for short fiction were The New Yorker and Playboy.
